blocks.text: But Chrysostom refutes this error as follows in Homily 12 on Matthew: Ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ φύσει, τὸ δὲ ἐν ὄψει περιστερᾶς ἐφάνη· [Ho men en tē hēmetera physei, to de en opsei peristeras ephanē] Christ appeared in our nature, but the Spirit in the form of a dove. Again: Ὁ μὲν υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ φύσιν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέλαβε· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα οὐ φύσιν ἀνέλαβε περιστερᾶς. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Εὐαγγελιστὴς οὐκ εἶπεν, ὅτι ἐν φύσει περιστερᾶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς· οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ μετὰ ταῦτα ὤφθη ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι, ἀλλὰ τότε μόνον. [Ho men huios tou Theou physin anthrōpou anelabe; to de pneuma ou physin anelabe peristeras. Dia touto kai ho Euangelistēs ouk eipen, hoti en physei peristeras, all' en eidei peristeras; oukoun oude meta tauta ōphthē en toutō tō schēmati, alla tote monon.] The Son of God took on the nature of a man, but the Spirit did not take on the nature of a dove. Therefore the Evangelist did not say that he (descended) in the nature of a dove, but in the form of a dove. [col. 37] Nor did he appear in that form afterwards, but only then. Augustine, however, who was wholly free of this error, believed only that a real dove, created by God for this purpose, was the symbol of the presence of the Holy Spirit. This is a much lighter error. For although this opinion cannot be reconciled with the words of the Evangelists, it differs from the former in that it contains nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Holy Spirit; for, without detriment to his dignity, he could be signified as well by a real dove as by the image of a dove. Fourth, it should be noted that Augustine's argument, by which he tries to prove that this was a real dove, has little force. We believe, he says, that both those bodies, namely those of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, were real bodies. For just as it was not fitting that the Son of God should deceive men, so it was not proper that the Holy Spirit should deceive men. I grant this. But I deny that anyone saw this form of a dove except Christ himself, Matth. III, 16. and Marc. I, 10., and John, Ioh. I, 32. Christ was indeed baptized in the midst of the crowds, Luc. III, 21., but no one has written that the dove appeared to them. And that it was seen by no one apart from Christ except John is plainly taught by Ioh. I, 32.: John bore witness to him, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and he remained upon him. For what need would there have been of the testimony of so great a [II, 571] man to prove what others too had seen, indeed all the crowds that then stood around Christ and John? Moreover, this form of a dove did not deceive Christ, who was free from error; nor John, who had been forewarned by God that his Spirit would descend in visible form and remain upon his Son, and so, when he saw this form of a dove descend and settle upon Christ, he knew for certain that this was taking place in a vision, as God had foretold. Accordingly he does not say that he saw a dove, but as it were a dove. Yet even supposing, without conceding it, that this φάσμα [phasma] of a dove was seen by all and was believed by most to have been a real dove, not even so would the Holy Spirit have deceived them. For he does not truly deceive who places an image before the eyes with the intention not of deceiving but of teaching. Such was this vision, in which the form of a dove was set before the eyes, not so that it should be believed to be a real dove, but so that through it the presence of the Holy Spirit, and what his powers are, might be signified. If this is held to be falsehood, the use of all visions will be abolished, in which one thing is shown to the eyes and another to the mind. And the Holy Spirit would then have deceived not only in the vision of the dove but also in that of the fiery tongues. For those tongues were not real tongues, nor was it real fire. Accordingly, just as here he is said to have descended ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ [hōsei peristera], so there the tongues are said to have been seen ὡσεὶ πυρὸς [hōsei pyros], Act. II, 3. And a little before, a sound is said to have been heard, not of wind, but as of wind, ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας [hōsper pheromenēs pnoēs biaias], so that we may know that all these things happened in a vision.

I cannot refrain from adding that the Hebrews too, in Cant. II, 12., understand the Holy Spirit by the name of the turtledove, a bird of the dove kind. Hence the words of the sacred text, The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land, are paraphrased by the Chaldee thus: וקול רוחא דקודשא דפורקנא דאמרית לאברהם אביכון כבר שמעתון And the voice of the Holy Spirit, that is, the deliverance which I foretold to Abraham, your father, Gen. XV, 14. 16., you have already heard. Origen too refers these very words to the Holy Spirit, who, he holds, is signified by the turtledove when he reveals more hidden things, and by the dove when he teaches things better suited to the understanding of the common people. The Holy Spirit, he says, when he speaks of great and more hidden mysteries, which many cannot grasp, is designated by the name of the turtledove, that is, of that bird which always dwells on mountain ridges and in the tops of trees. But in the valleys, and in those things which reach down to men, the dove is taken. So he writes on the words of the Canticle: The voice of the turtledove, etc. [col. 38]
